about: Reviewed facts: where a historical boundary followed a river or wall, on which stretch and when. Read by scripts/build-hist-courses.mjs. `reviewed` may move a coarse line; `notDrawn` may not: each says what the research found (`verdict`) and why it is not drawn — refuted, undetermined, or confirmed but not placeable within 1 km on a modern line.

reviewed.claim: After Basil II's reconquest the southern bank of the lower Danube (Paristrion/Paradounavon, roughly Moesia Inferior and Dobruja) was a Byzantine frontier province, and the river separated it from the Pechenegs 'who dwelt beyond the Danube'. Stephenson accepts that Basil II extended the empire's political borders 'as far as the Danube', creating 'a frontier between Byzantium and the turbulent lands beyond the Danube'; Dall'Aglio, following Madgearu, calls the river a 'permeable frontier' guarded by forts.
reviewed.channel: Upstream of the delta the main channel is broadly where it was, but between Calarasi/Silistra and Braila the river is braided (Borcea arm west of the Balta Ialomitei, main 'Old Danube' east of it) and no source says which arm bounded Paristrion; do not snap to the Borcea. Below Isaccea/Tulcea (the delta) the medieval outlets differ from today's (the Sulina arm is a 19th-century canalised course), so the stretch deliberately stops at Isaccea.
reviewed.review: Accepted from Vidin (taken 1002, Stephenson p. 65) to Durostorum/Silistra, the seat of Paristrion. Not drawn below Silistra: between Calarasi and Braila the river is braided (Borcea arm vs main arm) and no source says which arm bounded the province.

sources.cite: Paul Stephenson, Byzantium's Balkan Frontier: A Political Study of the Northern Balkans, 900-1204, Cambridge University Press, 2000, pp. 6-7, 63-65, 89-91, 98, 318
sources.supports: Basil II extended the political borders as far as the Danube; recovery of Pliska/Preslav (1001) and Vidin (1002); Pechenegs crossing the frozen river into Paristrion (1047) and nomads settled south of the Danube; 'The loss of Paradounavon' from 1072; conclusion: a frontier between Byzantium and the lands beyond the Danube.

sources.cite: Francesco Dall'Aglio, 'Paristrion as Centre and Periphery: from Byzantine Border Province to Heartland of the Second Bulgarian Tsardom', Studia Ceranea 12, 2022 (doi 10.18778/2084-140X.12.12), abstract and p. 5
sources.supports: Paristrion was a Byzantine border province on the lower Danube after Tzimiskes and Basil II; with the Pechenegs north of the Danube the river became a 'permeable frontier' (citing Madgearu); mixobarbaroi employed to defend the 'Danube limes'.

sides.name: Ottoman Empire (directly ruled sanjaks of Vidin, Nikopol, Silistra)

reviewed.claim: The lower Danube separated directly ruled Ottoman territory from the tributary principality of Wallachia. The Ottomans also held fortified districts (kaza/raya) on the left bank at Turnu, Giurgiu and later Braila until the Treaty of Adrianople (1829); after that the Danube itself 'formed the border between the Wallachian voivodeship and the Ottoman state'. Giurgiu is described as lying on the northern border of the Ottoman Empire.
reviewed.channel: Between Calarasi/Silistra and Braila the river is braided (Borcea arm vs main arm, Balta Ialomitei and Balta Brailei). No source says which arm was the limit, and the Balta was drained and regulated in the 20th century.

exceptions.place: Turnu (Turnu Magurele) raya on the left bank, Ottoman 1420-1829
Giurgiu raya on the left bank (c. 25 villages), Ottoman by 1449-1829

reviewed.review: The edge of direct Ottoman rule against tributary Wallachia from the Timok mouth to Silistra. Ends at the Treaty of Adrianople (1829-09-14), which returned the left-bank rayas; the rayas of Turnu and Giurgiu are kept coarse (their extent is not established). Only the Ottoman side is redrawn: Cliopatria's Wallachia carries no verified identity. Not drawn below Silistra (braided reach; Braila raya from 1538/42).

sources.cite: TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi, 'Yergogu' (Giurgiu)
sources.supports: Giurgiu on the left bank; taken 1420 (not 1417); Wallachian in 1427; Ottoman by 1449; after the 1829 Edirne treaty the Danube formed the Wallachian-Ottoman border.

sources.cite: Meryem Kacan Erdogan, 'An Ottoman Castle on the North Border in the XVIth Century: Giurgiu', Balkan Arastirma Enstitusu Dergisi (Trakya University) 11/1, 2022
sources.supports: Giurgiu on the left bank of the Danube, on the northern border of the Ottoman Empire, directly affected by Ottoman-Wallachian relations.

sources.supports: Wallachian rayas on the northern bank around Turnu, Giurgiu and Braila; returned in 1829.

reviewed.claim: Scholarship describes the Polish-Moldavian boundary as running for most of its course along the White Cheremosh, the Kolachin and the Dniester, and the Dniester as Moldavia's eastern boundary from the late 14th century. On the middle Dniester (Khotyn opposite Kamianets) the river is therefore the boundary between Moldavia and Poland/Lithuania. The southern terminus on the left bank (Yahorlyk brook, beyond which lay Crimean/Ottoman Yedisan) is attested only by a Wikipedia summary of Romanian historiography.
reviewed.channel: Gorge reach without known avulsion; the Novodnistrovsk (1981) and Dubasari (1954) reservoirs are narrow and follow the old valley.
reviewed.review: Moldavia's eastern boundary on the Dniester, from where the Kolachin line reaches the river to the Yahorlyk mouth. Both opened sources state that the boundary ran along the Dniester (Wasiucionek; Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, which dates Moldavia's reach to the river to the late 14th century, so 1400 is the latest year that statement allows). Ends at the Treaty of Buczacz (1672-10-18). Only Moldavia's side is redrawn (the far bank changed hands).

sources.cite: Michał Wasiucionek, 'Across the Dniester: The Texture of Contact in the Seventeenth-Century Polish-Moldavian Borderland', Polish History (polishhistory.pl)
sources.supports: the boundary ran for most of its course along the White Cheremosh, the Kolachin and the Dniester

sources.cite: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine, 'Moldavia'
sources.supports: Moldavia bounded by the Dniester to the east; by the late 14th century it extended to the Dniester

sources.cite: Wikipedia, 'History of Transnistria to 1792' (cites Ion Nistor and Aurel V. Sava) - used only to locate the Yahorlyk terminus
sources.supports: left bank north Lithuanian (Podolia), south Crimean/Ottoman Yedisan from 1504; the border between them on the Yahorlyk brook

reviewed.claim: After invading Chosŏn in 1627 the Manchus concluded a covenant that emphasised the Yalu as the boundary and required each state to guard its own territory; later Korean crossings for ginseng were treated as trespass. Song (2017) treats the Yalu section as the long-established western boundary, and Bohnet speaks of 'the established boundaries of Chosŏn at the Yalu and Tumen' (while noting precise demarcation came only in the 18th century).
reviewed.channel: As for the Ming period: branching and island accretion on the lower 40 km around Sinuiju/Dandong; middle course impounded by 20th-c. dams. Today's main channel is adequate at ~5 km precision.
reviewed.review: The 1627 covenant named the Yalu as the boundary (Liu & Piao 2020, citing the Injo sillok). Drawn from Uiju upstream to Manp'o only: below Uiju the islands and the choice of branch were disputed until the 20th century, so a precise channel there would claim an allocation that did not exist.

sources.cite: Jing Liu and Yan Piao, 'Expansion, Contestation, and Boundary Making: Chosŏn Korea and Ming China's Border Relations over the Yalu River Region', International Journal of Korean History 25(2), 2020, pp. 105-142
sources.supports: 1627 covenant with the Manchus emphasised the Yalu River as the boundary and required each state to guard its territory; Willow Palisade later fenced the Yalu region

sources.cite: Nianshen Song, 'The Journey towards "No Man's Land": Interpreting the China-Korea Borderland within Imperial and Colonial Contexts', Journal of Asian Studies 76(4), 2017
sources.supports: Yalu section of the boundary dates from the late 14th century; Qing patrolled the border with Korea

sources.cite: Adam C. I. Bohnet, Migrant and Border Subjects in Late Chosŏn Korea, PhD thesis, University of Toronto, 2008, pp. 37-43, 119-120
sources.supports: Chosŏn's 'established boundaries' at the Yalu and Tumen; lower Yalu one of Chosŏn's more stable land frontiers

reviewed.claim: The Encyclopedia of Korean Culture and Liu Yang (2017) state that by the mid-15th century Chosŏn's northern limit 'fully extended' to the Yalu and that a riverside defence system made the Yalu main stream the boundary. Upstream of Uiju the far bank was Jianzhou Jurchen country, not Ming-administered, so the river was Chosŏn's defended limit facing tribal polities rather than a bilateral state boundary.
reviewed.channel: Middle Yalu now impounded by the Sup'ung (1941) and later dams; reservoirs fill the old valley, so the historical line lies within ~1 km of the drowned channel.
reviewed.review: Joseon's northern limit on the middle Yalu, completed with the Four Commanderies (1443) and the Six Garrisons (1449); both sources state that by the mid-15th century the limit reached the Yalu and that a riverside defence system held it. The far bank was Jurchen country without a state, so only Joseon's side is redrawn. Ends with the proclamation of the Later Jin (1616).

sources.supports: Through the 4 commanderies and 6 garrisons Korea's northern boundary 'fully extended' to the Tumen and Yalu banks

reviewed.claim: The 1372 treaty treats the Morava as the river dividing Austria north of the Danube from Pozsony County, with fishing rights shared fifty-fifty, and the 1411 confirmation states that the March is the border between Hungary and Austria. The Österreich-Lexikon states that until 1918 the March was the border with the Hungarian half of the monarchy.
reviewed.channel: Meandering river regulated 1935-1980s: 23 meander cut-offs and trenches on the lower Morava; the historical boundary followed the pre-regulation meanders, not today's straightened channel in cut-off reaches.
reviewed.review: The 1372 border treaty and its 1411 confirmation state that the March is the boundary between Austria and Hungary, from the Thaya mouth at Hohenau to the Danube below Devin (Skorka 2019). The river was straightened 1935-1980s; in the cut-off meanders the historical line lay on the old channel, within about 1 km of the drawn one.

sources.cite: Renáta Skorka, 'On Two Sides of the Border: The Hungarian-Austrian Border Treaty of 1372', Hungarian Historical Review 8 no. 2 (2019), pp. 302-303
sources.supports: Morava divided Austria north of the Danube from Pozsony County (1372); 1411: the March is the border between Hungary and Austria

feature.name: Danube (Iron Gates and Dacia Ripensis section)

reviewed.claim: After Dacia was evacuated the Danube between Singidunum and the Olt again became the frontier, now of the new province Dacia Ripensis, reorganised in the late 3rd and 4th centuries, restored by Justinian and lost to Avar and Slav invasions in the early 7th century.
reviewed.channel: Iron Gates section submerged by the Iron Gate I and II reservoirs (1972, 1984); otherwise mostly stable rock-confined course; floodplain sections downstream of Kladovo with islands.

exceptions.place: Drobeta (Turnu Severin), late Roman fortification on the north bank
Hinova, late Roman fortification on the north bank
Desa, late Roman fortification on the north bank

reviewed.review: From the abandonment of Dacia (271) to the Avar-Slav collapse of the limes (614): the Danube from the head of the Iron Gates (Golubac) to the Olt. Not drawn upstream of Golubac (Singidunum-Viminacium lies in the Pannonian floodplain, where no source places the Roman channel). The Iron Gates reservoirs (1972, 1984) follow the gorge in plan. The late north-bank fortifications are kept coarse. The right-bank Roman and Byzantine fortresses of the lower Danube (Bononia/Vidin, Ratiaria, Oescus, Novae, Sexaginta Prista, Transmarisca, Durostorum) stand on the river today: the river still runs under the southern bluff it ran under then.

sources.cite: D.J. Breeze, S. Jilek, M. Korac et al., Frontiers of the Roman Empire: Roman Limes in Serbia, Archaeopress, 2022, p. 43, p. 45, p. 47
sources.supports: Aurelian's decision (274) to withdraw from Dacia; frontier reorganised; Hunnic invasion 441-443; Justinian's restoration; frontier completely overrun in 614.

feature.name: Danube (lower Danube, Moesia Inferior / Moesia Secunda / Scythia)

reviewed.claim: From Hadrian to the early 7th century the lower Danube was the frontier of Moesia Inferior (later Moesia Secunda and Scythia), with legionary fortresses at Oescus, Novae, Durostorum and Troesmis; it survived the 5th century and was restored under Justinian before Avar and Slav invasions ended it. Downstream of Durostorum the installations stood on the higher ground 'along the most easterly river channel'.
reviewed.channel: Downstream of Durostorum the river develops many twisting channels in a wide zone (Balta Ialomitei / Braila marshes); the Roman line follows the easternmost channel (Macin branch side), not necessarily today's main navigation channel. Changes >1 km likely in the Braila marsh section.

exceptions.place: Daphne, Constantinian bridgehead on the left bank opposite Transmarisca/Tutrakan (site approximate)

reviewed.review: From Hadrian's withdrawal from the plain north of the lower Danube (118) to 614: the Olt mouth to Durostorum/Silistra. Not drawn between Silistra and Braila (braided Balta reach; the Roman line followed the easternmost arm, not today's main channel). The right-bank Roman and Byzantine fortresses of the lower Danube (Bononia/Vidin, Ratiaria, Oescus, Novae, Sexaginta Prista, Transmarisca, Durostorum) stand on the river today: the river still runs under the southern bluff it ran under then.

reviewed.claim: The Danube was the boundary of Raetia, Noricum and Pannonia for over 400 years from the 1st century AD, with a continuous chain of military installations 'almost all along the southern banks of the river', defined continuously from the Flavian period, and broke down in the 5th century. In Raetia new auxiliary forts on the Danube were set up under Vespasian (Eining, Regensburg, Straubing, Passau); from c. 150 the Raetian land limes met the Danube at Hienheim near Eining, so the river was the frontier only downstream of that point.
reviewed.channel: YES in places: UNESCO notes the Danube 'has shifted its course considerably since Roman times' in places and in places the original course 'has not been identified'. Major regulation at Vienna (19th c.) and in the Hungarian plain; the Szigetkoez/Bratislava inland delta and the Gemenc floodplain are areas of large shifts.
reviewed.review: The Norican Danube in its confined valley from Batavis/Passau to Lentia/Linz (the Schlögen meander). Only the bedrock-confined reaches of the western segment are drawn: UNESCO (property 1608) records that elsewhere the Danube has shifted considerably since Roman times and in places its Roman course has not been identified (Straubing basin, Vienna, the Szigetköz inland delta, the Gemenc floodplain).

sources.supports: First continuously defined in the Flavian dynasty (69-96 CE); continuous chain of installations almost all along the southern banks; for more than 400 years the middle European boundary; broke down in the 5th century; bridgehead on the left bank; river shifted its course considerably in places.

reviewed.claim: From the early 1st century AD to the early 5th century the Lower Rhine between Remagen and the delta was the boundary of the province of Lower Germany, held by a chain of forts on the left (west) bank roughly 10 km apart, and described by Breeze et al. as 'the first frontier of the Roman world to reach the classical shape of a continuous chain of forts'. The Upper Germanic Limes volume states that after AD 9 'the Lower Rhine remained the frontier of the empire's territory until Late Antiquity'. In the 4th century the frontier was repeatedly reinstated (Constantine c. 310, Julian, Valentinian, Theodosius).
reviewed.channel: Partly. Downstream of Bonn the Roman river 'meandered more freely, migrating within its band of holocene sediments, about 3 km wide'; forts were placed on the terrace edge where meanders touched it. Several Roman sites now lie away from the present channel (individual shifts not quantified in the sources consulted). 19th-20th-century regularisation fixed the present bed. Upstream of Bonn (Middle Rhine gorge) the course is stable.
reviewed.review: The Rhine below the Vinxtbach (the Germania Inferior boundary) through the Middle Rhine gorge to Bonna/Bonn, where the course is stable. Not drawn below Bonn: there the Roman river meandered within a holocene belt about 3 km wide and several Roman sites now lie away from the channel. Ends with the crossing of December 406.

notDrawn.why: It is a boundary of spheres agreed between two powers, not a garrisoned line, and the east bank was largely the kingdom of Osrhoene (a Parthian client), not Parthia directly. Downstream of the Sura area the river valley was Parthian on both banks (Dura-Europos, on the west bank, was Parthian until 165), so the river was NOT the boundary there. Upstream of the Turkish-Syrian border the west bank was the client kingdom of Commagene (independent vassal until 38, annexed again later), so the Roman provincial boundary there is not the river for most of this period. The dataset end of 215 is refuted: the river ceased to be the external boundary on this stretch from 165 (formally c. 195-200).
